summary:
Sri Lanka's Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex activity under Section 365, covering "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", and Section 365A, covering "gross indecency", with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment. Section 365 was applied to men; Section 365A was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, and both provisions are recorded as applying to men and women. Where the offence is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the aggravated penalty is ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Prosecutions are rare but the provisions structure everyday policing. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 country research recorded no convictions under the articles, while Outright International reports that harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services remain frequent, and the US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBT victims, particularly allegations of sexual violence or blackmail, citing Section 365 as justification, and human-rights organisations have documented officers using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBT individuals.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct. The practice is widely condemned as torture. No comprehensive anti-discrimination protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity is in place.

The International Commission of Jurists reported in August 2023 that the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, and that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission had acknowledged this in recent months. The accompanying legal argument is that administrative circulars cannot substitute for statutory reform.

Legal gender recognition is available. The Ministry of Health issued a circular in 2016 to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, and a recognised identity card has been issued since June 2016. No surgical intervention is legally required, though the certification process is bureaucratic and may be onerous.

Detention carries specific exposure. Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing; Media Spokesperson and Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake stated in October 2024 that current facilities make it impossible to give transgender prisoners their own space and that separate accommodation is planned only for prisons built in the future. Placement by birth sex remains the practical default within the existing male and female ward system, and no statutory placement rule exists.

Trans detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to their preferred gender where possible. Those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender, after which the inmate's own preference feeds the accommodation decision. Officials have given as an explicit reason for resisting gender-based placement their concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing with male offenders. The exception process is therefore discretionary and medicalised rather than codified.

Access to gender-affirming care is limited. Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible because many hospitals lack the highly specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report "All Five Fingers are Not the Same" said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. Patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and even ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, which raises treatment costs; obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught.

Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages or same-sex civil unions and does not provide equal rights to same-sex live-in couples. The marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that same-sex marriages are not a human right.
tangentialFactors:
The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as "risky behaviour" alongside drug use and having multiple partners.

The UK Home Office published a Country Policy and Information Note on Sri Lanka covering sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, version 6.0 of September 2024, which assesses risk from state and non-state actors, protection available, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims. A joint stakeholder report submitted for the country's third Universal Periodic Review cycle, produced by EQUAL GROUND with academic and Geneva-based human-rights partners, documents criminalisation and violations against LGBTIQ individuals.

Public attitudes do not track the statutory position. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed, while a 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else and 51.4% would support rights legislation. A 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents identified as LGBTQI.

Legislative movement on conversion therapy has stalled. In March 2022 SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban the practice, which she said the government had failed to support as of July 2024; despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer "treatment" to LGBTQ family members.
localsOnly:
Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, and politicians from both major parties have expressed support for LGBTQ rights. The influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter has backed rights extension and a constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times described as the first such public acknowledgement by a head of state in the region.

Community organisations include Companions on a Journey, founded in 1994 as the country's first LGBTQ support group, the Women's Support Group founded in 1999, and Equal Ground. Even so, Section 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

The Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners has asked that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space, including possible space within prison hospitals, citing that developed countries have recognised transgender rights. As of October 2024 no codified placement policy existed, and the official route ran through an identity card where held and a doctor's assessment where not.

In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy, after which the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that unlike psychiatrists, counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Sri Lanka was not retrievable at research time, returning HTTP 403; its underlying documentation of the criminalisation of same-sex activity is therefore unverified here and is not drawn on in this record.

Several medical and policing findings above rest on reference-site country coverage rather than primary documentation, including the account of the 2016 Ministry of Health circular's downstream effects, the blood-donation restriction, patient reports of staff ridicule and the polling figures. They should be treated as unconfirmed against primary sources.

No sourced material addresses entry screening, visa refusal, airport or immigration treatment of transgender travellers, or whether gender markers on passports are checked on arrival; that risk layer is not covered by the current inventory.

No findings on youth-specific access to care appear in the sources. Nor is there sourced evidence on whether the ten-year penalty has ever been imposed in a case involving transgender identity specifically, or on the existence of any hate-crime sentencing enhancement for bias-motivated violence against transgender persons.
